# Kosambakakkhandhaka (Kd 10)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kosambakakkhandhaka* is the tenth chapter of the *Mahāvagga* in the Vinaya Piṭaka's Khandhaka section [Horner, Book of the Discipline Vol. VI; Prebish 1994; Sung 1999]. The text addresses disputes and splits in the monastic community, opening with the narrative of the "Kosambī incident". In an effort to reconcile the quarreling monks, the Buddha recounts the story of Dīghāvu (an expanded version of the *Kosambīya Jātaka*); when this fails to resolve the division, he departs to visit the venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila, who model concord and communal harmony. In monastic jurisprudence, the chapter treats offences of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) and procedural suspensions (*ukkhepaniyakamma*) imposed for failing to acknowledge an offence, make amends, or relinquish a wrong view [Horner, Book of the Discipline Vol. VI]. The commentary *Samantapāsādikā* refers back to this chapter regarding monastic advantages and procedures for suspended monks [Horner, Book of the Discipline Vol. VI].

Curated cross-tradition parallels include the *Kośāmbakavastu* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya (preserved in Sanskrit, Tibetan, and Chinese), as well as corresponding Khandhaka chapters in the Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, and Sarvāstivāda Vinayas [Prebish 1994]. Specific narrative episodes and verses correspond directly to the *Upakkilesa Sutta* (MN 128 / MĀ 72), the *Dīghītikosalajātaka* (Ja 371) and *Kosambiyajātaka* (Ja 428), verses in the Dhammapada, Udāna, and Theragāthā, and the *Khaggavisāṇa Sutta* (Snp 1.3). DharmaNexus algorithmic matching aligns the Pali text strongly with the Sanskrit *Kośāmbakavastu* (SA_K01_vinv09_u) and Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D0001-3), as well as Chinese Āgamas (MĀ 72 and EĀ 24.8), the Patna Dharmapada, and the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records substantial textual reuse with MN 128, the *Saṁghabhedakakkhandhaka* (Kd 17), the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), and the *Parivāra* (Pvr 15 and 17) [DharmaNexus].
